title: Content tracing: examining fact-checking via a WhatsApp group during the COVID-19 pandemic
screen_reason: The abstract reports a content analysis of a defined corpus with a denominator (238 forwarded messages sent to a public fact-checking WhatsApp group in Singapore over the first six months of COVID-19) and an accuracy verdict on that corpus: 'nearly half of the messages were either partly or entirely inaccurate'. That is a share of items classified inaccurate, so CONTENT — but the share is stated only as 'nearly half', so the row carries value_kind range_not_point with no point value, and the denominator is a user-selected, suspicion-driven set (messages people chose to submit for fact-checking), not messages people received.

estimates.date: First six months of the COVID-19 pandemic in Singapore (approximately January-June 2020; exact dates not given in the abstract)
estimates.measure_type: % of messages forwarded to a public WhatsApp fact-checking group that were partly or entirely inaccurate
estimates.value_raw: "nearly half of the messages were either partly or entirely inaccurate" (of 238 forwarded messages)
estimates.denominator: 238 messages forwarded by users to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore during the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic
estimates.definition: Message coded on 'facticity' as partly inaccurate or entirely inaccurate (versus accurate); exact coding rules not recoverable from the abstract.
estimates.misinfo_def: Not given in the abstract; the operative category is messages 'either partly or entirely inaccurate' as judged in the authors' content analysis of facticity.
estimates.source_quote: This study is based on a content analysis of 238 forwarded messages sent to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore during the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic to understand what types of information people would submit for fact-checking, allowing insights into possible motivations behind the use of fact-checking services. Focusing on content characteristics, we examined the range of topics, valence, and facticity of the messages forwarded to the WhatsApp group to be fact-checked. The most common topic was public policy and action; most of the messages focused on negative aspects; and nearly half of the messages were either partly or entirely inaccurate.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Not determinable from the abstract. The abstract says the authors 'examined the range of topics, valence, and facticity of the messages', which reads as researcher content coding; it is possible the facticity codes follow the fact-checking group's own verdicts. No coder count and no reliability statistic available.
estimates.moderator_quote: This study is based on a content analysis of 238 forwarded messages sent to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore during the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic to understand what types of information people would submit for fact-checking
estimates.notes: Three warnings for an adjudicator. (1) No point value: 'nearly half' is the only figure the abstract gives, so value_kind is range_not_point and value_pct is empty; the full text presumably prints the exact share. (2) The denominator is SELECTION-BY-SUSPICION: these are messages users chose to send to a fact-checking service, so the corpus is enriched for doubtful content and the share must not be read as the prevalence of inaccuracy in Singaporean WhatsApp traffic. denom_selection=curated flags that; the group is also a single channel, so single_source would apply equally — curated is the more consequential flag. (3) breadth=misleading because the numerator merges 'partly' with 'entirely' inaccurate. The abstract also reports the share rose over the six months, but gives no period-specific numbers, so no time-sliced rows are possible.

missed_or_uncertain: Working from the abstract alone. Not extractable: the topic distribution ('the most common topic was public policy and action'), valence ('most of the messages focused on negative aspects'), and the temporal trend ('the messages shared to be authenticated ... contained more inaccuracies' as the situation worsened) — all reported without numbers in the abstract. The exact inaccuracy percentage, the split between 'partly' and 'entirely' inaccurate, the coder count and any reliability statistic, and the precise data-collection dates all require the full text. If the full text is obtained, this row should be replaced with the exact value and the breadth re-checked (an 'entirely inaccurate' only figure would be breadth=false).

rob.design: Content analysis of 238 messages forwarded by members of the public to a public fact-checking group on WhatsApp in Singapore over the first six months of the COVID-19 pandemic; corpus is a census of submissions to that one group, so participation is self-selected and no response rate applies. Coding covered topic, valence and facticity. Number of coders, codebook and intercoder reliability are not reported in the abstract and the full text was not available.
rob.item6_quote: Focusing on content characteristics, we examined the range of topics, valence, and facticity of the messages forwarded to the WhatsApp group to be fact-checked.
